source.title_on_document: Small-world Networks of Agents Brainstorm AI Risks

supplement.holds: Implementation details; system-variant and stakeholder-seeding results (Tables 2-3); practitioner benchmark demographics (Table 4); control and treatment risk reports (Figures 5-6); rubric correlation matrix (Figure 7). No additional human-study arm sizes or uncertainty statistics are supplied.

paper_design_summary: The first evaluation compares LLM risk-generation configurations using expert-rated risks from a separate corpus produced by 45 AI practitioners, with generated risks mapped to that corpus (p. 6, Sections 4.1-4.3; p. 15, Table 2). In the human assistance study, 11 teams comprising 40 young, predominantly non-Western chatbot users were randomly assigned to practitioner-generated or LLM-framework-generated starting risk reports, then brainstormed chatbot harms using the Futures Wheel (p. 9, Section 5.1). Their outputs were counted overall, by consequence layer, and by risk category (p. 9, Section 5.2 and Figure 4).

studies.label: Evaluation 1: system-configuration benchmark using practitioner-generated risks

assignment.what_was_assigned: System configurations vary network topology, stakeholder discovery, and centrality ranking. No allocation of human participants to AI-assistance conditions is described in this evaluation; practitioner outputs provide a reference corpus.
assignment.quote: To evaluate those two baselines and our framework, we mapped all system-generated risks to practitioners-generated risks using a two-stage process combining embedding-based similarity and manual validation.

participants.who: The reference corpus was produced by 45 AI practitioners, including company workers, researchers, and students, in 8 blank-slate workshops. It contains 244 risks, of which 108 were matched to system outputs for evaluation; the number of people contributing those matched risks is not stated. Five external AI-domain experts supplied ratings. These source-corpus authors and raters are separate from the randomized Futures Wheel sample (p. 6, Sections 4.1-4.3; p. 14, A.3; p. 16, Table 4).
participants.quote: We recruited 45 AI practitioners across 3 locations via mailing lists, online ads, and EventBrite.
participants.locator: p. 6, Sections 4.1-4.3; p. 14, A.3; p. 16, Table 4. The reported analyses compare system configurations using matched risks, not a reported count of people analyzed under AI-assistance conditions.

ai_tool.name_model: LLM stakeholder-network framework extending Plurals; underlying LLM name/version not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Simulated stakeholder agents generate and propagate risks through alternative network structures; centrality metrics rank risks. The human reference corpus supplies expert ratings through semantic matching and manual validation (p. 6, Sections 4.2-4.3; p. 14, A.1).

task.description: Generate and prioritize possible harms of AI chatbot companions; benchmark generated risks against expert-rated practitioner risk statements (p. 6, Sections 4.1-4.3).
task.duration: Practitioner reference workshops lasted 1 hour and 45 minutes each (p. 6, Section 4.1); system-run duration not stated.

outcomes.name: Novelty of generated risks matched to the practitioner benchmark
outcomes.question: none

contrasts.reported: Small-world + Betweenness, Snowballing Typical Roles: Novelty 3.48; Single-turn LLM: Novelty 2.32. Scores are normalized to a five-point Likert scale. This is a system-versus-system comparison using matched practitioner-risk annotations; no uncertainty statistic is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 2, Small-World Network + Betweenness Centrality / Snowballing Typical Roles and Baselines / Single-turn LLM; p. 6, Sections 4.2-4.3 for scoring and matching.

studies.label: Evaluation 2: team-randomized Futures Wheel ideation workshop

assignment.what_was_assigned: Teams were assigned to receive a practitioner-generated risk report (control) or a report with the same number of risks generated by the small-world LLM framework (treatment) as starting material for ideation.
assignment.quote: The teams were randomly assigned to two conditions:
assignment.locator: p. 9, Section 5.1, Experimental Conditions: Practitioners-Seeded (Control) vs. Framework-Seeded Ideation (Treatment).

arms.name: Practitioners-seeded (control)
arms.description: Five teams received a report containing risks brainstormed by AI practitioners in the first evaluation. People per arm are not reported; the team count is not a people count (p. 9, Section 5.1; p. 17, Figure 5).

arms.name: Framework-seeded (treatment)
arms.description: Six teams received a report containing the same number of risks, generated by the small-world stakeholder-network framework. People per arm are not reported; the team count is not a people count (p. 9, Section 5.1; p. 18, Figure 6).

participants.who: Young, frequent chatbot users from predominantly non-Western backgrounds. The reported sample comprises 40 people in 11 teams, with three to four people per team; the text says all teams conducted the exercise. No separate post-exclusion analysis count or people counts by arm are given (p. 9, Section 5.1).
participants.quote: We recruited 11 teams of participants, comprising a total of 40 individuals (with three to four people per team).
participants.locator: p. 9, Section 5.1, Participant Demographics and Recruitment and Experimental Conditions; Section 5.2 and Figure 4 report team-level results.

ai_tool.name_model: Small-world network of LLM stakeholder agents, implemented by extending Plurals; underlying LLM name/version not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Treatment teams received a report of pre-generated risks sampled from the framework's prioritized risk set and used it to begin Futures Wheel ideation. Control teams received practitioner-generated examples (p. 9, Section 5.1; p. 14, A.1; pp. 17-18, Figures 5-6).

task.description: Teams brainstormed harms of AI chatbot companions using the Futures Wheel, tracing immediate, secondary, and tertiary consequences from supplied risk reports (pp. 8-9, Sections 5 and 5.1).

outcomes.name: Risk fluency overall and by Futures Wheel consequence layer
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Average risks per team: treatment 21.1 versus control 15.6. Level 1: treatment 5.2 versus control 5.2; Level 2: treatment 8.7 versus control 5.2; Level 3: treatment 7.2 versus control 5.2. Figure 4A shows capped error bars for both conditions at each consequence layer. Error-bar type: null; numerical error-bar values: null, because neither is specified in the text or caption. No numerical SD, SE, confidence interval, test statistic, or p-value is supplied.

outcomes.name: Risk counts within MIT AI Risk taxonomy categories
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Average risks per team, treatment versus control: Human-Computer Interaction 8.2 vs. 6.0; Socioeconomic & Environmental harms 5.6 vs. 2.4; AI System Safety Failures & Limitations 3.5 vs. 0.0. Privacy & Security is printed in control-versus-treatment order: 1.5 vs. 1.0. These are counts of risks within categories, not a count of distinct categories or similarity across people. No uncertainty statistic is reported.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Govers et al. (2026), When and How AI Should Assist Brainstorming for AI Impact Assessment. S1 reuses the practitioner-workshop dataset as its reference corpus. The document does not report reuse of the randomized Futures Wheel sample (S2).
sample_overlap.quote: To evaluate our framework, we drew on a dataset from 8 human-based brainstorming workshops focused on identifying risks associated with AI chatbot companions
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 6, Section 4.1, opening sentence; p. 12, References, Govers et al. (2026).

company_involvement.description: Ke Zhou, Edyta Bogucka, and Daniele Quercia all list Nokia Bell Labs, UK as an author affiliation. This establishes company involvement through authorship; no separate company funding or sponsorship arrangement is stated.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1, author names, affiliation superscripts, and affiliation 1 (Nokia Bell Labs, UK).

eligibility.reason: The human assistance study explicitly randomly assigns 11 teams comprising 40 people to LLM-generated versus practitioner-generated starting reports (p. 9, Section 5.1). Its risk counts are scored on team outputs (p. 9, Section 5.2 and Figure 4), but its 40-person sample is below 50, so it is excluded from core and retained only in the screening report. The first evaluation reports comparisons among model configurations using an expert-rated human reference corpus; its 45 source practitioners and five raters are separate from the randomized sample and cannot be added to meet the threshold (p. 6, Sections 4.1-4.3; p. 15, Table 2).

one_line_finding: In a randomized study of 40 people in 11 teams, teams given LLM-framework risk reports averaged 21.1 risks versus 15.6 with practitioner reports, but the study falls below the 50-person core threshold (p. 9, Sections 5.1-5.2).
